g.text: Many objects share one append-only file, and a local index holds the offsets
Derived, not assumed: a drive gives 100-150 random IOPS regardless of size, and the cluster holds 675 million objects.
One sealed 4 GB file, holding many objects end to end
Retention and deletion become unlink() and rewrite, never an in-place edit - the file is append-only, so you cannot punch
a hole in the middle of it. That single fact is what makes compaction the only way space comes back.
The per-node offset index - deliberately local, not a cluster service
object_mapping (SQLite or RocksDB, on the data node)
Why local rather than a shared cluster index
A data node only ever answers questions about data it holds. A shared
index would add a network round trip to every read for information the
node could have stored locally - and would have to absorb the full
cluster read rate, becoming a bottleneck and a shared failure domain
for a lookup that is intrinsically local. Keeping it local means it
scales with node count and dies with the node it describes.
Not a hash map in memory: it must survive restart without re-scanning
4 GB files to rebuild offsets, and compaction needs a range scan.
The same ordering rule, one layer down
Record the location first and a crash leaves an index
entry pointing at bytes that never landed - a dangling
pointer that reads as corruption. This way a crash leaves
bytes nothing references: harmless, reclaimed next pass.
Compaction - how space actually comes back
Only SEALED files are compacted - the active file has a moving tail.
The index update is ONE transaction, and the source is unlinked only
after it commits, so a crash mid-compaction leaves the index pointing
at the old file, which still exists. Crash-safe by construction.
